name: Kenya
governanceModel: A published national AI strategy plus a pending, ambitiously-scoped AI Bill proposing a dedicated Commissioner, layered on an existing Data Protection Act already tested against AI-adjacent companies

overview:
Kenya has moved further than most African peers toward a comprehensive, dedicated AI governance framework, while also being a focal point for global debate over the labour conditions underlying AI's supply chain. The Ministry of Information, Communications and the Digital Economy (MICDE), under Cabinet Secretary William Kabogo, launched Kenya's first National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (2025-2030) in March 2025, organised around AI digital infrastructure, data ecosystems and governance, and research/innovation/commercialisation. In February 2026, nominated Senator Karen Nyamu introduced the Artificial Intelligence Bill, 2026, which would create an Office of the AI Commissioner as an independent regulator with powers to inspect AI systems, access training data, maintain a public registry of high-risk applications and enforce a four-tier risk classification — a more centralized model than the sector-based approaches taken by South Africa or (so far) Nigeria. Separately, the ministry opened a fresh, broader public consultation on a draft Kenya Artificial Intelligence and Other Emerging Technologies Policy in mid-2026, with written submissions due by August 4, 2026.

Alongside this policy activity, Kenya's role as a hub for the global AI data-labelling and content-moderation workforce has produced some of the continent's highest-profile AI-adjacent litigation. More than 180 former Meta and Sama content moderators and data annotators have pursued cases in Kenyan courts since 2022 alleging unlawful dismissal, exploitative pay and conditions, and (in 2026 reporting) exposure to intimate footage captured by Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses during content review work. Kenyan courts have repeatedly ruled that Meta can be sued locally despite jurisdictional objections, though as of mid-2026 a full trial date had still not been firmly set.

atAGlance.regulatoryApproach: A risk-tiered, centralized model proposed under the pending AI Bill (new AI Commissioner), alongside a broader AI & Emerging Technologies Policy still in public consultation
atAGlance.latestMajorUpdate: Ministry of Information, Communications and the Digital Economy opens public participation on the draft Kenya AI and Other Emerging Technologies Policy, with submissions due August 4, 2026
atAGlance.governmentInvolvement: High — a dedicated national strategy, a pending AI-specific bill proposing a new regulator, and an existing Data Protection Commissioner already engaging with AI-related privacy questions
atAGlance.industrialStrategy: National AI Strategy (2025-2030) prioritising health, agriculture, education, finance and public services, plus Konza/Technopolis-linked digital hubs and BPO-style AI-assisted platforms
atAGlance.internationalPartnerships: Strathmore University's CIPIT engages internationally on AI governance research (e.g., with the Alan Turing Institute), and Kenya remains a major hub for outsourced AI data-labelling work for global technology firms
atAGlance.primaryPolicyFocus: Advancing the Artificial Intelligence Bill, 2026 through Parliament while finalizing the separate, broader AI and Emerging Technologies Policy following its 2026 public consultation

currentDirection.summary: Kenya's direction in 2026 has been toward more formal, centralized AI oversight: the Artificial Intelligence Bill, 2026 proposes a new Office of the AI Commissioner with inspection, investigation and registry powers, and the ministry's parallel AI and Emerging Technologies Policy consultation (running into August 2026) signals continued momentum. At the same time, unresolved litigation over Meta- and Sama-linked content moderation and data-labelling work continues to shape international scrutiny of Kenya's AI-adjacent labour practices, a dimension largely separate from the formal legislative track.

recentDevelopments.text: Reporting notes that the draft Kenya AI and Other Emerging Technologies Policy — whose public-participation window closed on 4 August 2026 — includes proposed occupational-protection standards for AI data workers, covering minimum pay, access to mental-healthcare support and safeguards against exposure to harmful content, a nod to Kenya's prominence as a data-labelling and content-moderation hub.

Ministry of Information, Communications and the Digital Economy opens public participation on the draft Kenya Artificial Intelligence and Other Emerging Technologies Policy, with written submissions due by August 4, 2026.

President William Ruto signs the Technopolis Act, replacing the Konza Technopolis Development Authority with a new Technopolis Development Authority overseeing Kenya's planned tech-city infrastructure.

The proposed $1 billion Microsoft-G42 geothermal-powered AI data centre at Olkaria (announced with KenGen in 2025) stalls after the government declines to guarantee the up-to-1GW of power and offtake the facility would require; President Ruto acknowledges Kenya's grid cannot support it at full scale, and officials float 'captive power' arrangements as a possible path forward.

Reporting details Meta's termination of its Sama content-review contract following complaints that moderators were exposed to intimate footage recorded by Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses; Sama subsequently lays off more than 1,000 Kenyan employees.

Nairobi courts continue hearing the Meta/Sama content-moderator cases; rulings on procedural matters are repeatedly postponed, delaying a full trial on claims from more than 180 former moderators and data annotators.
Nominated Senator Karen Nyamu introduces the Artificial Intelligence Bill, 2026, proposing a new Office of the Artificial Intelligence Commissioner with risk-based regulatory powers.
Ministry of Information, Communications, and Digital Economy launches Kenya's first National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (2025-2030) at KICC, Nairobi.

policyAndRegulation.title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025-2030
policyAndRegulation.summary: Kenya's first national AI strategy, launched March 2025, organised around AI digital infrastructure, data ecosystems/governance, and research/innovation/commercialisation, with cross-cutting focus on ethics, skills, finance and governance.

policyAndRegulation.title: Data Protection Act, 2019
policyAndRegulation.summary: General data-protection law enforced by the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner (ODPC), already applied to AI-adjacent disputes and cited as the legal basis the proposed AI Bill would build upon rather than replace.

policyAndRegulation.title: Artificial Intelligence Bill, 2026
policyAndRegulation.summary: Sponsored by nominated Senator Karen Nyamu; would create an Office of the AI Commissioner with powers to inspect AI systems and training data, maintain a public high-risk AI registry, and enforce a four-tier risk classification, plus penalties (up to KES 5 million and prison terms) for non-consensual deepfakes. Must pass both houses of Parliament and receive presidential assent before taking effect; as of mid-2026 it remains under review, with legal commentators questioning overlap with the Data Protection Commissioner and Communications Authority.

policyAndRegulation.title: Kenya Artificial Intelligence and Other Emerging Technologies Policy
policyAndRegulation.summary: Broader draft policy covering AI and other emerging technologies, under development since around November 2025 by MICDE; public submissions were open through August 4, 2026, as part of a five-phase drafting process.

researchEcosystem.summary: Kenyan AI policy research is led substantially by Strathmore University's Centre for Intellectual Property and Information Technology Law (CIPIT), which conducts research on AI governance, ethics and regulation from an African perspective and convenes the Conference on the State of Artificial Intelligence in Africa (COSAA). KICTANet, a Nairobi-based multi-stakeholder think-tank network, is also active in mapping Kenya's AI ecosystem and has engaged in international partnerships on responsible AI (including with the UK's Alan Turing Institute).

notableGaps.note: No frontier foundation-model developer is headquartered in Kenya; the country's global AI footprint is concentrated in outsourced data-labelling/content-moderation work and applied fintech/agritech AI rather than model development.

As of mid-2026, both the Artificial Intelligence Bill, 2026 and the broader AI and Emerging Technologies Policy remain in draft/consultation stages, so no dedicated binding AI statute is yet in force.

debates.topic: Kenyan content moderators' and data annotators' court battles with Meta and Sama over AI-related labour conditions
debates.summary: More than 180 former Meta/Sama content moderators and data labellers have pursued Kenyan court cases since 2022 alleging unlawful dismissal, low pay and inadequate mental-health support, with 2026 reporting adding claims about exposure to intimate footage from Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses.
debates.expanded: Kenyan courts have repeatedly rejected Meta's jurisdictional objections, allowing the cases to proceed, but a full trial date remained unset as of early 2026 after further procedural postponements. The dispute has become a reference point in global debates about the labour conditions underlying AI content-moderation and data-annotation supply chains, with Kenya's position as a major outsourcing hub for this work drawing sustained international scrutiny alongside its ambitions to be recognised as a broader AI innovation hub.

debates.topic: Whether Kenya's proposed AI Commissioner would duplicate the Data Protection Commissioner and Communications Authority
debates.summary: Legal commentators have questioned whether the Artificial Intelligence Bill, 2026's proposed Office of the AI Commissioner would create bureaucratic overlap with Kenya's existing Data Protection Commissioner and Communications Authority.
debates.expanded: The bill grants the proposed Commissioner broad powers — inspecting AI systems, accessing training data, maintaining a high-risk AI registry — on top of an existing regulatory landscape already shaped by the 2019 Data Protection Act and the 2018 Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act (the latter having already been used by Kenyan courts to halt Worldcoin's iris-scanning operations). Some business groups have also raised concerns about compliance costs for smaller AI-related SMEs under a new, strict regulatory regime.
